1 OurBigBook.com
Regard K as a vector space over F. Since K is finite, a maximal linearly independent list has finite length d and is a basis. Every element is uniquely a linear combination of its d basis vectors, with q choices for each coefficient. Hence ∣K∣=qd​, with d=[K:F]. This includes d=1 when the extension is trivial.

Words: 102 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 102
2 OurBigBook.com
Write q=pr, where p is the characteristic. In a splitting field of Xqm−X over F, let K be its set of roots. The derivative of this polynomial is −1, so all qm roots are distinct. The Frobenius power is additive and multiplicative: (x+y)qm=xqm+yqm and (xy)qm=xqmyqm. Thus roots are closed under addition, negatives and multiplication; for a nonzero root, (x−1)qm=x−1. They include 0,1 and form a field.
Every a∈F satisfies aq=a, by Lagrange's theorem on F× and separately at zero. Iterating gives aqm=a, so F⊆K. The constructed field therefore contains F and has exactly qm elements​.

Solution
Words: 56
3 OurBigBook.com
By the allowed cyclicity theorem, K× has a generator z. Every nonzero element of K is a power of z, and zero also belongs to F(z). Thus K⊆F(z)⊆K, giving K=F(z)​. This is a primitive element argument for finite fields using the multiplicative group, not a claim that the additive group is cyclic.

For α=0, Lagrange's theorem in the multiplicative group of order qm−1 gives αqm−1=1; at zero the desired identity is immediate. Thus all elements satisfy αqm−α=0.
For an irreducible degree-m polynomial f∈F[X], the quotient L=F[X]/(f) is a field of dimension m, hence has qm elements by part 1. Its element α=[X] therefore satisfies αqm−α=0. The evaluation homomorphism F[X]→L has kernel (f), so
f(X)∣Xqm−X.​

a OurBigBook.com
Given N⊴G and H≤G, the conditions are G=NH,N∩H={1}​. Every element then has a unique expression nh. The extra datum is the action α:H→Aut(N) given by conjugation, αh​(n)=hnh−1. On pairs (n,h) the reconstructed multiplication is
(n,h)(n′,h′)=(nαh​(n′),hh′).
(2)
For example S3​=⟨(123)⟩⋊⟨(12)⟩. The order-three subgroup is normal, the intersection is trivial, and their sizes multiply to six. Conjugation by (12) inverts (123), so the action is nontrivial. Consequently this is not the direct product of these subgroups: C3​×C2​ is Abelian, whereas S3​ is not.

Compose the second map first. Direct substitution gives
(A,b)(A′,b′)=(AA′,Ab′+b).​
(3)
The result is affine because the product matrix is invertible. The identity is (I,0) and the inverse is (A−1,−A−1b). Associativity follows from composition of maps, or by expanding this product three times. Distinct pairs give distinct maps, since evaluating at zero gives b and evaluating the difference on basis vectors gives all columns of A. Thus these pairs faithfully describe a group.

The map A↦(A,0) is an injective group homomorphism, so its image is the required copy of GLn​(F). Translations are the subgroup N={(I,b):b∈Fn}, isomorphic to the additive group of Fn. For any affine map,
(A,b)(I,t)(A,b)−1=(I,At).​
(4)
Thus conjugation preserves translations, proving N⊴G.

Every pair factors as (A,b)=(I,b)(A,0), and a linear map which is also a translation fixes zero and has linear part I, hence is the identity. Thus G=NH and N∩H={1}. The conjugation formula in (c) says that the action needed for reconstruction is simply the usual matrix action A:t↦At on the additive group Fn. Therefore
G≅Fn⋊GLn​(F).​
(5)

There are pn choices for the translation. Choose the columns of an invertible matrix successively: the first is any nonzero column, the second avoids its span, and at stage j+1 one avoids a j-dimensional span of size pj. Consequently
∣G∣=pnj=0∏n−1​(pn−pj).​
(6)
The successive linear independence conditions are exactly the criterion that the columns form a basis.

A primitive root modulo p is a generator of the cyclic multiplicative group (Z/pZ)×, so it has order p−1. If g is one generator, the generators are exactly gk with gcd(k,p−1)=1. Hence there are ϕ(p−1)​. For p=2 the group is trivial and its unique element is its generator, consistently with ϕ(1)=1.

Words: 105 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 105
ii OurBigBook.com
For n≥1, the zero residue contributes zero. Multiplication by any nonzero α permutes the nonzero residues, so the sum S satisfies S=αnS in Fp​. If p−1∤n, choose a primitive root α; then αn=1, forcing S=0. If p−1∣n, every nonzero term equals one, so S=p−1=−1 in the field.
The printed display also mentions n=0, although its introductory assumption is n≥1. For that extra case the sum of the p integer values x0 for 1≤x≤p is p≡0, so that branch is consistent too. The result is
x=1∑p​xn≡−1(modp) exactly when n>0, (p−1)∣n;0 otherwise.​
(7)

The Legendre symbol being one means a is nonzero and a square modulo p. Take one root r=0. Factoring x2−r2=(x−r)(x+r) in the field shows that any root is r or −r. Since p is odd these are distinct. Thus there are exactly 2​ solutions.

Solution

iv OurBigBook.com
Each nonzero quadratic residue is attained twice as x2 for 1≤x≤p−1. Therefore twice the sum of those residues is ∑x=1p−1​x2, which is zero modulo p by (ii), since p−1>2. As two is invertible modulo p, the sum of the residues is zero. The sum of all nonzero residues is p(p−1)/2≡0, so subtracting gives the same result for the nonresidues. Hence both indicated sums are 0(modp)​.

q∈{2,3,7,11,31}.​

D OurBigBook.com
The monotone convergence theorem states that if nonnegative measurable functions hn​ increase almost everywhere to h, then ∫h=limn​∫hn​, allowing infinity. The dominated convergence theorem states that if measurable hn​→h almost everywhere and ∣hn​∣≤g for an integrable g, then h is integrable and ∫hn​→∫h.

Words: 59 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 59
1 OurBigBook.com
Apply monotone convergence to An​=∑k=1n​∣ak​∣. Its limit A=∑k≥1​∣ak​∣ has integral ∑k​∫∣ak​∣<∞, so A<∞ almost everywhere. Thus the original series converges absolutely almost everywhere. Its partial sums are bounded in absolute value by the integrable function A, and their limit s satisfies ∣s∣≤A. Dominated convergence gives
∫s=nlim​k=1∑n​∫ak​=k=1∑∞​∫ak​.​
(9)
Assigning any value on the null exceptional set defines an integrable representative of s.

For 0<x<1, expand (1−x)−2=∑k≥1​kxk−1. All terms after multiplication by (logx)2 are nonnegative, so monotone convergence permits integration term by term. Substituting x=e−t and integrating by parts twice gives
∫01​xk−1(logx)2dx=∫0∞​e−ktt2dt=k32​.
(10)
Consequently the integral is ∑k≥1​2/k2, and the supplied sum gives π2/3​.

D OurBigBook.com
A sufficient differentiation theorem is the following local version. Suppose u(t,⋅) is integrable, u(⋅,x) is continuously differentiable for almost every x, and for each compact parameter interval there is an integrable g(x) bounding ∣∂t​u(t,x)∣ uniformly there. Then I′(t)=∫E​∂t​u(t,x)dx. The mean value theorem bounds the difference quotients by g, and dominated convergence proves the formula. Integrability at one parameter value together with the derivative bound also suffices locally.

A subset A is connected if, with its subspace topology, it cannot be written as A=U∪V with U,V disjoint nonempty relatively open sets. Equivalently its only subsets both open and closed relative to A are ∅,A. This definition includes the empty set and singletons as connected sets.

The connected subsets of the real line are exactly the intervals, including singletons, unbounded intervals and the empty set. Equivalently, whenever x<y belong to the set, every z with x<z<y also belongs to it. Endpoints may or may not be included.

Choose one nonempty Ai0​​; every other Ai​ intersects it and must lie on that same side. Thus the other side is empty, a contradiction. If the union is empty it is connected by definition. Therefore i⋃​Ai​ is connected​.

Ka​=⋃{S⊆X:S connected, a∈S}​

Words: 81 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 81
iii OurBigBook.com
The inclusion of X into R is continuous, so a connected component K of X is an interval in R. For x∈K, openness of X gives ε>0 with (x−ε,x+ε)⊆X. This interval is connected and meets K, so their union is connected and maximality forces the interval into K. Thus K is open in R. A nonempty open connected subset of the line is an open interval, allowing an infinite endpoint or the whole line. Hence every component is an open interval.

iv OurBigBook.com
The components cover X and are pairwise disjoint by (b)(ii); by (iii) they are open intervals. Each nonempty interval contains a rational number. Enumerate the rationals and assign to each interval the first rational it contains. Disjointness makes these assigned rationals distinct, giving an injection from the set of components into N. Thus X is a countable union of pairwise disjoint open intervals​, with the empty union for X=∅.

i OurBigBook.com
A subset K is compact if every cover of K by sets open in the ambient space has a finite subcover. Equivalently, every relatively open cover of the subspace K has a finite subcover. These agree because relatively open sets are intersections with ambient open sets.

Words: 43 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 43
ii OurBigBook.com
A subset B of a metric space is bounded if it lies in a ball of finite radius: there exist a point x0​ and R<∞ such that d(x,x0​)≤R for every x∈B. Equivalently its diameter supx,y∈B​d(x,y) is finite, with the empty set bounded by convention.
iii
Words: 206 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 206
iii OurBigBook.com
In any topological space a closed subset of a compact set is compact: add its open complement to an open cover and take a finite subcover of the compact set. However, compact subsets need not be closed in a general space. In the indiscrete two-point space a singleton is compact but not closed. Conversely a closed subset need not be compact: R itself is closed in R but the cover {(−n,n):n≥1} has no finite subcover.
In a Hausdorff space every compact subset K is closed. Given x∈/K, separate x and each k∈K by disjoint neighborhoods; compactness selects finitely many neighborhoods covering K, and the intersection of their companion neighborhoods of x misses K. Thus the complement is open. Closedness still need not imply compactness, as the same real-line example shows. It does imply compactness if the ambient space is compact.
In a metric space compactness implies boundedness: finitely many radius-one balls cover the set, so their centers have a finite maximal distance from any fixed center and the triangle inequality gives a global bound. The converse is false. An infinite set with discrete metric d(x,y)=1 for x=y is bounded, but its singleton cover has no finite subcover. It is even closed and complete, so closedness plus boundedness alone does not suffice in general metric spaces.

Words: 43 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 43
iv OurBigBook.com
By the Heine–Borel theorem a subset of R is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded. Consequently the nonempty compact intervals are exactly [a,b](−∞<a≤b<∞)​. This includes the degenerate interval [a,a]. The empty interval is compact as well; nonclosed bounded intervals and all unbounded intervals fail the criterion.

Words: 120 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 120
v OurBigBook.com
The image f(K) is compact: pull any open cover back by the continuous map, use a finite subcover of K, then map forward. For a general topological target, closedness is not guaranteed; a continuous image into the indiscrete two-point space can be a nonclosed singleton. No connectedness assertion follows merely from compactness of K.
If Y is metric, f(K) is compact, therefore closed in Y, bounded and totally bounded. It is also complete in its induced metric and sequentially compact. For the latter properties, compact metric spaces have a convergent subsequence of every sequence; a Cauchy sequence with one convergent subsequence converges to that same limit. Total boundedness follows by selecting finitely many balls of each prescribed radius. These are properties of the image itself, irrespective of whether Y is complete.

A metric space is complete if every Cauchy sequence of its points converges to a point of that same space. The requirement on the location of the limit distinguishes, for example, R from its incomplete subspace Q.

Yes. A Cauchy sequence of continuous functions in the supremum norm is Cauchy in the given complete space of bounded functions, so it has a uniform limit there. A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous: at a point, use two uniform errors smaller than ε/3 and continuity of one sufficiently late term for the remaining error. Thus the limit is in C([0,1]), proving completeness. Equivalently this is a closed subspace of the given complete space.

η=−ξcotξ,η2+ξ2=2mV0​a2/ℏ2.​

In the required sketch, the second equation is a first-quadrant circle arc of radius R=2mV0​a2​/ℏ. The curve −ξcotξ starts with limiting value −1 at zero, rises to zero at π/2, and then rises to +∞ as ξ↑π. Thus a positive-η intersection in this range must have ξ>π/2. The accompanying plot shows the circle below threshold and one above it.
Consequently R<π/2 rules out all odd states: the first positive branch already requires that radius, and later branches require still larger ξ. This is precisely 2mV0​<(πℏ/(2a))2​. At equality the intersection has η=0 and would not decay at infinity, so it too is not a normalizable bound state. An odd state first appears only for a strict increase beyond threshold.

An arbitrary orthonormal basis does not have the printed property. For example on [−1,1] with w=1, take the usual normalized constant and linear Legendre polynomials and swap their labels p0​,p1​. The resulting family is still an orthonormal basis but p0​ has one zero, rather than zero. The necessary intended hypothesis is that pk​ has degree k, or equivalently that the basis is obtained by orthogonalizing 1,x,x2,… in that order.
Under this hypothesis, pk​ is orthogonal to every polynomial of degree less than k. Let t1​,…,ts​ be its sign-changing zeros in (a,b) and put q(x)=∏j=1s​(x−tj​). If s<k, then pk​q has a constant nonzero sign except at finitely many points: each interior sign change has been canceled, and all remaining zeros have even multiplicity or occur at endpoints. Since w>0, its integral cannot vanish. But orthogonality to q, of degree s<k, says that integral is zero, a contradiction. Thus s≥k. Since the polynomial has degree k, it follows that
pk​ has exactly k distinct simple zeros, all in (a,b).​
(67)
This proves the requested conclusion in its standard intended setting and explains why it does not follow from the literal basis statement alone.

Solution
Words: 190
i OurBigBook.com
Encode a labelled tree by repeatedly deleting its smallest-labelled leaf of a graph and recording its neighbor, stopping when two vertices remain. This produces a sequence of length n−2 with entries in {1,…,n}.
Conversely, given such a sequence, at each step choose the smallest unused label not occurring in the remaining sequence, join it to the first sequence entry, delete that chosen label and the first entry, and continue. Finally join the two labels left over. A label outside the remaining sequence always exists because two more labels than entries remain. The process never uses a previously deleted label as a sequence entry. Each step attaches a new leaf of a graph to the eventual remaining graph, so backward induction shows that the result is connected and acyclic, hence a tree.
In a tree encoding, a vertex occurs once for every incident edge except the edge by which it is eventually removed, or the final surviving edge. Thus its number of occurrences is its degree minus one. The labels absent from the current remaining sequence are exactly the current leaves of a graph. Both procedures therefore choose the same smallest leaf of a graph and edge at every stage. They are inverse maps, proving the claimed bijection, including the empty sequence when n=2.

{13,14,15,12,26,27,28,89,8−10}.​

Independently draw Y∼q and U∼Uniform(0,1). Accept Y if U≤p(Y)/(Mq(Y)); otherwise discard it and repeat with fresh independent draws. Return the first accepted value. Solution
Words: 201
a OurBigBook.com
Recursively sort two halves, then merge their increasing lists by repeatedly choosing the smaller current first element. The following function preserves repetitions, as sorting a vector should:
R
merge_sort <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  stopifnot(n >= 1L)
  if (n == 1L) return(x)
  m <- n %/% 2L
  left <- merge_sort(x[seq_len(m)])
  right <- merge_sort(x[(m + 1L):n])
  nl <- length(left)
  nr <- length(right)
  out <- integer(n)
  i <- j <- k <- 1L
  while (i <= nl && j <= nr) {
    if (left[i] <= right[j]) {
      out[k] <- left[i]
      i <- i + 1L
    } else {
      out[k] <- right[j]
      j <- j + 1L
    }
    k <- k + 1L
  }
  if (i <= nl) out[k:n] <- left[i:nl]
  if (j <= nr) out[k:n] <- right[j:nr]
  out
}
Induction proves correctness: each recursive result is sorted and preserves its input multiset; each merge step removes the least remaining element from one of them, so the output is sorted and has exactly the union multiset. The base case has length one. Each merge takes linear time, yielding O(nlogn) time overall. Choosing from the left first on a tie makes the sort stable. The required input is an integer vector without missing values.

Here f′(x)=4x3−12x2+4x+12 and f′′(x)=12x2−24x+4. This implementation uses the undamped Newton step, checks a stationary point's curvature, and reports failure on a two-cycle or exhausted iteration limit:
R
newton_min <- function(x0, tol = 1e-10, maxit = 100L) {
  fp <- function(x) 4*x^3 - 12*x^2 + 4*x + 12
  fpp <- function(x) 12*x^2 - 24*x + 4
  x <- x0
  trace <- x
  for (k in seq_len(maxit)) {
    g <- fp(x)
    h <- fpp(x)
    if (abs(g) <= tol) {
      return(list(x = x, converged = h > 0,
                  reason = if (h > 0) "minimum" else "not a strict minimum",
                  trace = trace))
    }
    if (!is.finite(h) || abs(h) <= .Machine$double.eps)
      stop("Newton step has zero or invalid curvature")
    next_x <- x - g/h
    if (!is.finite(next_x)) stop("Nonfinite Newton iterate")
    trace <- c(trace, next_x)
    n <- length(trace)
    if (n >= 3L && abs(trace[n] - trace[n - 2L]) <= tol*(1 + abs(next_x)))
      return(list(x = next_x, converged = FALSE,
                  reason = "two-cycle", trace = trace))
    x <- next_x
  }
  list(x = x, converged = FALSE, reason = "iteration limit", trace = trace)
}
A sufficiently close start near −0.7692923542 converges to the minimum. The derivative cubic has exactly one real root: after x=1+t it is proportional to t3−2t+2, whose local maximum and minimum are both positive, so it crosses zero only once, on the left. Since the quartic tends to +∞ in both directions and its curvature at that stationary point is positive, this is the unique global minimum. The function reports convergence rather than assuming that every starting point must reach it.
